lessons.title: ਫਿਰ (phir) — "again," the seed of "see you again"

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page

segments.text: One small word turns a goodbye from "farewell" into "till next time."
ਫ (pha, an aspirated p) + ਿ (the sihārī, i-sign) + ਰ (ra) becomes ਫਿਰ (phir).
Only ਰ is yours to read so far. The other two pieces are shapes to notice, not to decode: a later session in this chapter teaches them.

ਫਿਰ (phir) means "again, then, afterwards" — a native Indo-Aryan adverb (the same word as Hindi phir) with no tidy English cognate, but a familiar job: it turns a parting into a promise. English "see you again," Punjabi phir milāṁge ("we'll meet again").

segments.instruction: "phir" — mind the aspirated ph
what it adds to a goodbye ("again / then")
segments.source: [YOU SAY: what it adds to a goodbye ("again / then")]

segments.text: A future-tense verb — the other half of "see you again."
ਮਿ (mi) + ਲਾਂ (lāṁ, la + long ā + nasal) + ਗੇ (ge) becomes ਮਿਲਾਂਗੇ (milāṁge).
You already read ਮ and ਲ. The rest are shapes to notice for now.
ਮਿਲਾਂਗੇ (milāṁge, "we will meet") is the future of milṇā ("to meet, to be found"), from Sanskrit mil- ("to join, unite") — the root of milāp ("a union, meeting").

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the future is an ending

segments.text: Punjabi marks the future with an ending on the stem: mil- ("meet") + -āṁge ("we will") becomes milāṁge. No helper-word like English "will" — the tense lives in the ending.

segments.instruction: "milāṁge"
the root and its cousin-noun (mil- "to join," milāp "a meeting")
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the root and its cousin-noun (*mil-* "to join," *milāp* "a meeting")]

segments.text: What verb is milāṁge from, and how does Punjabi mark "will"? (Milṇā "to meet," from Sanskrit mil-; with the ending -āṁge, not a separate word.)

segments.prompt: Say (we) will meet aloud, then type the romanized word and the ending that carries will.

feedback.correct: Right: the future rides on -āṁge, with no separate word for will.
feedback.incorrect: Say milāṁge — the future is the ending -āṁge on the stem mil-.

segments.text: The warm, everyday goodbye — where Chapter 1's sat srī akāl is the formal one.

ਫਿਰ ਮਿਲਾਂਗੇ = ਫਿਰ (phir, "again") + ਮਿਲਾਂਗੇ (milāṁge, "we will meet") — "we'll meet again." Chapter 1 gave you sat srī akāl, the Sikh greeting that doubles as a formal goodbye; phir milāṁge is the everyday, hopeful one — the same "promise of return" the whole subcontinent prefers to a blunt farewell (Hindi phir milenge, Bengali āshi, Tamil pōy varugiṟēṉ). Even more casual: phir mildē hāṁ ("(we) meet again," present for a near future).

segments.text: A tender Punjabi goodbye — one that puts you in God's care.
ਰੱਬ (rabb, "God" — note the addak doubling on ੱਬ) + ਰਾਖਾ (rākhā, "keeper, protector"). Both words open with the ਰ you already read.

ਰੱਬ ਰਾਖਾ means "[may] God [be your] keeper" — rabb ("God") + rākhā ("protector," from rakhṇā, "to keep, protect," from Sanskrit rakṣ-, "to guard," the root of rākṣas and of English-borrowed rakhi). The word for God, ਰੱਬ (rabb), is itself telling: it is Arabic rabb ("lord, master") — the same rabb of Arabic rabb al-ʿālamīn ("Lord of the worlds"). So this most Punjabi of farewells fuses an Arabic name for God with a Sanskrit verb of keeping — Punjabi's two vocabularies in one blessing. Warmer still: rabb rākhā, phir milāṁge ("God keep you, we'll meet again").

lessons.title: ਫ, ਗ, ਿ — three pieces met inside a word you already say
lessons.gloss: three pieces of Gurmukhi, met inside a word you already say

needs: a pen and something to write on

notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called Script you'll notice: ਫ, ਗ, ਿ until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: The first word of this chapter is three pieces long, and the last one arrives today.
First, say the last things you learned once more, out loud and from memory:

segments.instruction: ṭhīk, koī gall nahīṁ

segments.text: ਫ.
phapphā — pha. A consonant with a puff of breath after it — p plus an audible h, not the f of English phone.
ਗ.
gaggā — ga. A consonant, the voiced g of go, with no breath after it.
sihārī — -i. A mātrā for short i, and the one that surprises everybody: it is written before the consonant it is spoken after.
Now put them where you have already heard them:
ਫ + ਿ + ਰ becomes ਫਿਰ (phir).
ਫਿਰ — phir — again, then.
You are not being asked to write any of this. You are being asked to recognise it the next time it goes past.

blocks.title: Writing: copy what you can see

segments.text: Keep ਫ, ਗ, ਿ in front of you and do not cover any of them. Follow each shape once with a finger, then copy it once with a pencil, larger than it is printed. Say its sound as your hand stops.
This is observe-and-trace with the model visible. Nothing in these chapters asks you to write a Punjabi word from memory; that ladder starts later, and it starts from these same shapes.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — roots you now carry

segments.text: milāṁge from mil- "to join" (milāp, "a meeting").
rabb from Arabic "Lord/God"; rākhā from Sanskrit rakṣ- "to protect".
the future -āṁge ending — "we will," carried in the verb.
You're leaving a friend and expect to see them soon. Give the warm goodbye, then bless them on the way. (Phir milāṁge — and rabb rākhā.)
Independent Gurmukhi reading and writing are not scored here. Romanization is evidence for spoken recall only; a typed romanization never counts as Gurmukhi writing.
